cards.front: Why can the stretches of a complete gut specialize, and what must happen to large food molecules along it?
cards.back: Food moves one way, so each stretch can do its own job. Large molecules must be broken down before or within the stretch that can absorb them; what is not absorbed moves on.
cards.quote: A complete gut is a one-way line, so its stretches can specialize.

cards.front: Which dietary substances need no breakdown before absorption, and which sugars must be split first?
cards.back: Water, salts and single sugars (monosaccharides) need none. Sugars of two or more units, starch included, must be split first.
cards.quote: Water, salts and single sugars (monosaccharides) need no breakdown; sugars of two or more units, starch included, must be split first.

cards.front: Enzymatic hydrolysis splits large molecules (starch, proteins, fats) into small subunits by {{c1::adding water}} across their bonds.
cards.quote: Enzymatic hydrolysis splits large molecules (starch, proteins, fats) into small subunits by adding water across their bonds.
cards.section: One tube, four jobs and two helpers

cards.front: How do bile salts speed the digestion of dietary fat, and is bile an enzyme?
cards.back: They emulsify fat: large drops break into small droplets that lipase can reach. Bile is not an enzyme; lipase does the hydrolysis.
cards.quote: Bile salts emulsify fat, breaking large drops into small droplets that lipase, the fat-digesting enzyme, can reach.
cards.section: One tube, four jobs and two helpers

cards.front: What can gut microbes do with food that the host's own enzymes cannot?
cards.back: With their own enzymes they split bonds the host has no enzyme for, then ferment the products, without oxygen.
cards.quote: With their own enzymes the microbes split bonds the host has no enzyme for, then ferment the products.
cards.section: One tube, four jobs and two helpers

cards.front: Contrast the gut of Hydra or a planarian with the gut of an earthworm, insect or vertebrate.
cards.back: Hydra and planarians have an incomplete gut: a sac with one opening (the gastrovascular cavity); leftovers leave the way food came in. The others have a complete, one-way tube from mouth to anus.
cards.quote: a sac with one opening, the gastrovascular cavity, where food is digested and the leftovers go out the way they came in.
cards.section: One tube, four jobs and two helpers

cards.front: Three pairs of major salivary glands (parotid, submandibular, sublingual) add saliva, whose {{c1::amylase}} starts digesting starch.
cards.quote: Three pairs of major salivary glands (parotid, submandibular, sublingual) add saliva, whose amylase starts digesting starch.
cards.section: Mouth to anus in a human

cards.front: In the human stomach, what do parietal cells and chief cells secrete?
cards.back: Parietal cells: hydrochloric acid. Chief cells: pepsinogen, the inactive form of pepsin, which starts protein digestion.
cards.quote: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and chief cells secrete pepsinogen, the inactive form of pepsin, which starts protein digestion.
cards.section: Mouth to anus in a human

cards.front: Waves of muscle contraction, called {{c1::peristalsis}}, push the swallowed lump (the bolus) to the stomach.
cards.quote: Waves of muscle contraction, called peristalsis, push the swallowed lump (the bolus) to the stomach.
cards.section: Mouth to anus in a human

cards.front: Which three structures multiply the absorptive surface of the human small intestine?
cards.back: Circular folds, finger-like villi, and the microvilli on each lining cell.
cards.why: The small intestine is the main site of digestion and nutrient absorption, so surface area matters there.
cards.quote: Circular folds, finger-like villi and the microvilli on each cell multiply its surface.
cards.section: Mouth to anus in a human

cards.front: What are the separate roles of the liver and the gallbladder in handling bile?
cards.back: The liver makes bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it.
cards.quote: The liver makes bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it.
cards.section: Mouth to anus in a human

cards.front: A person secretes too little bile salt into the duodenum. What happens to fat absorption, and why?
cards.back: It is greatly reduced. Without bile salts, fat is not emulsified into droplets lipase can reach, and the products of fat digestion are not gathered into micelles that carry them to the cell surface.
cards.quote: bile salts gather the products of fat digestion into tiny clusters, micelles, that carry them to the cell surface
cards.section: Mouth to anus in a human

cards.front: In the human small intestine, how does absorbed fat leave the villi, compared with absorbed monosaccharides and amino acids?
cards.back: Fat is mostly packaged into chylomicrons, which leave through lacteals (lymph vessels of the villi). Monosaccharides and amino acids mostly enter blood capillaries.
cards.quote: the fat particles it sent into lacteals are chylomicrons
cards.section: Mouth to anus in a human

cards.front: A glucose molecule is absorbed into a blood capillary of a villus. Which organ does that blood reach first, and by what vessel?
cards.back: The liver, through the hepatic portal vein.
cards.why: Blood from the villi capillaries, carrying most absorbed monosaccharides and amino acids, drains first to the liver.
cards.quote: drains first to the liver, through the hepatic portal vein
cards.section: Mouth to anus in a human

cards.front: About 9 L of water a day enters an adult human small intestine. Where does most of it come from?
cards.back: Mostly from the gut's own secretions (saliva, gastric juice, bile, pancreatic and intestinal juice), poured in and taken back; less comes from food and drink.
cards.quote: Most of it is the gut's own secretions, poured in and taken back.
cards.section: The water budget: the one idea in numbers

cards.front: Round-figure human water budget at steady state: 9.0 L/day enters the small intestine, which absorbs 90%; the colon absorbs 0.8 L/day. Find fecal water and overall absorption.
cards.back: Small intestine absorbs 9.0 × 0.90 = 8.1 L/day; 0.9 L/day passes to the colon. Fecal water = 0.9 − 0.8 = 0.1 L/day. Overall = 8.9 / 9.0 = 98.9%.
cards.quote: Total absorbed = 8.1 + 0.8 = 8.9 L per day, so overall absorption = 8.9 / 9.0 = 98.9%.
cards.section: The water budget: the one idea in numbers

cards.front: In the same model (9.0 L/day in, small intestine absorbs 8.1 L/day), the colon's absorption is halved from 0.8 to 0.4 L/day. By what factor does fecal water change, and what is overall absorption?
cards.back: Fecal water = 0.9 − 0.4 = 0.5 L/day, five times 0.1, not double. Overall absorption = 8.5 / 9.0 = 94.4%, a drop of only 4.4 percentage points.
cards.quote: Fecal water = 0.9 − 0.4 = 0.5 L per day, five times 0.1.
cards.section: The water budget: the one idea in numbers

cards.front: Why does fecal water change by a large factor when overall gut water absorption changes by only a few percent?
cards.back: Fecal water is a small leftover after two large subtractions (9.0 − 8.1 − 0.8 = 0.1 L/day), so a small change in either large flow is a large change in the leftover.
cards.quote: so a small change in either large flow is a large change in the leftover.
cards.section: The water budget: the one idea in numbers

cards.front: In the round-figure model (9.0 L/day into the small intestine), the small intestine's share falls from 90% to 89% while the colon still absorbs exactly 0.8 L/day. Find the flow into the colon and fecal water.
cards.back: Absorbed = 9.0 × 0.89 = 8.01 L/day; flow into colon = 0.99 L/day (was 0.90). Fecal water = 0.99 − 0.8 = 0.19 L/day, 1.9 times the 0.10 L/day before.
cards.why: A model result: a real colon has spare capacity and partly compensates.
cards.quote: raises the flow into the colon from 0.90 to 0.99 L per day and fecal water from 0.10 to 0.19 L
cards.section: The water budget: the one idea in numbers

cards.front: In the round-figure model (9.0 L/day in), a disorder cuts small-intestine water absorption to 80% while the colon absorbs a fixed 0.8 L/day. Find fecal water and overall absorption, and say why the body, not only the gut, loses water.
cards.back: Absorbed 9.0 × 0.80 = 7.2; colon receives 1.8; fecal water = 1.8 − 0.8 = 1.0 L/day, ten times 0.1. Overall = 8.0 / 9.0 = 88.9%. Most gut water is the body's own secretion, so failing to reclaim it drains the body.
cards.why: Rests on the water balance rule; a real colon partly compensates, so this is a model result.
cards.quote: And since most of the water is the gut's own, a gut that stops taking it back drains the body.
cards.section: The water budget: the one idea in numbers

cards.front: Humans make no cellulase. How do gut microbes let a host get energy from cellulose?
cards.back: Microbes ferment cellulose and other plant polysaccharides into short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate), which the host uses for energy.
cards.quote: The microbes ferment cellulose and other plant polysaccharides into short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate), which the host uses for energy.
cards.section: Where the microbes sit: cow, horse, rabbit, hoatzin

cards.front: Name the four compartments of a cow's single stomach and the one that secretes acid and enzymes.
cards.back: Rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum. The abomasum is the glandular, acid-secreting compartment, equivalent to a single stomach; the rumen and reticulum hold the fiber-digesting microbes.
cards.quote: the abomasum is the glandular compartment that secretes acid and enzymes, equivalent to a single stomach.
cards.section: Where the microbes sit: cow, horse, rabbit, hoatzin

cards.front: What separates a foregut fermenter from a hindgut fermenter? Give one example of each.
cards.back: Foregut fermenters ferment before the acid-secreting region (cow, kangaroo, hoatzin). Hindgut fermenters ferment after the small intestine (horse in cecum and colon, rabbit mainly in cecum).
cards.quote: Foregut fermenters ferment before the acid-secreting region.
cards.section: Where the microbes sit: cow, horse, rabbit, hoatzin

cards.front: Where does the hoatzin, a leaf-eating South American bird, ferment its food?
cards.back: In its crop, the enlarged pouch of the esophagus. A chicken's crop, by contrast, mainly stores food.
cards.quote: ferments leaves in its crop, the enlarged pouch of the esophagus where many birds store food.
cards.section: Where the microbes sit: cow, horse, rabbit, hoatzin

cards.front: A rabbit ferments grass in its cecum, after the small intestine. If it is prevented from eating its soft cecal pellets, what does it lose, and why?
cards.back: It loses the microbes and their protein, which would no longer pass through the stomach and small intestine, where microbial protein is recovered as amino acids. Those lie upstream of the cecum.
cards.quote: a nutrient must be supplied, by food or by microbes, before or within the stretch that can absorb it
cards.section: Essential depends on who is eating

cards.front: Fecal microbes from three horses are cultured without oxygen with the same starch load. Lactate is cleared, and short-chain fatty acids rise, in cultures from two donors but not the third. What does this show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: The donors' microbial communities differed in how they handled the same load under these culture conditions. It does not show how the third horse itself would fare, since a culture is not a living gut.
cards.why: Same input, different output points to the community; extrapolating to the animal needs a test in the animal.
cards.quote: The microbes ferment cellulose and other plant polysaccharides into short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate), which the host uses for energy.
cards.section: Where the microbes sit: cow, horse, rabbit, hoatzin

cards.front: What does the enteric nervous system do, and does it need the brain to do it?
cards.back: It is a network of nerve cells in the gut wall that runs local reflexes, such as peristalsis, by itself.
cards.quote: Its wall holds the enteric nervous system, a network of nerve cells that runs local reflexes, such as peristalsis, by itself.
cards.section: Nerves and hormones run the line

cards.front: What kind of signals do the vagus nerves add to the gut, and what is their effect on secretion?
cards.back: Parasympathetic signals, from the rest-and-digest division of the autonomic nervous system, which increase secretion.
cards.quote: add parasympathetic signals, from the rest-and-digest division of the autonomic nervous system, that increase secretion
cards.section: Nerves and hormones run the line

cards.front: Sham-fed dogs (esophagus opened at the neck, stomach fistula) secrete gastric juice when they eat. After both vagus nerves are cut, eating gives no juice, but meat put directly into the stomach still gives some. What do the two results show?
cards.back: Juice evoked by eating needs the vagus. Food in the stomach can drive secretion without the vagus, for example through the hormone gastrin.
cards.quote: Food in the stomach can drive secretion without the vagus, for example through gastrin, a hormone from G cells of the lower stomach lining.
cards.section: Nerves and hormones run the line

cards.front: Gastrin: which cells release it, what triggers it, and what does it do?
cards.back: G cells of the stomach lining, triggered by food (especially protein) in the stomach and by vagal input. It raises stomach acid, partly by releasing histamine from nearby cells.
cards.quote: Stomach: more acid, partly by releasing histamine from nearby cells
cards.section: Nerves and hormones run the line

cards.front: After a meal, acidic chyme enters the human duodenum. Which hormone rises, and what response neutralizes the acid?
cards.back: Secretin, from the duodenal lining, rises. It drives pancreatic duct cells to secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid, and bicarbonate neutralizes the stomach's acid.
cards.quote: It sends digestive enzymes and bicarbonate, which neutralizes the stomach's acid, into the duodenum.
cards.section: Mouth to anus in a human

cards.front: CCK (cholecystokinin): where is it made, what triggers it, and what are its two main targets?
cards.back: The duodenal lining, triggered by fats and proteins in the duodenum. Pancreas: secretes enzymes. Gallbladder: contracts and releases bile.
cards.quote: Pancreas: enzymes; gallbladder: contracts, releases bile
cards.section: Nerves and hormones run the line

cards.front: A drug blocks CCK receptors. Predict the effect on digesting and absorbing a fatty meal, and trace the reasoning.
cards.back: Fat digestion and absorption fall. Less gallbladder contraction means less bile, so less emulsification and fewer micelles; less pancreatic enzyme output means less lipase.
cards.why: Combines CCK's targets with the roles of bile salts and lipase; no new facts.
cards.quote: Pancreas: enzymes; gallbladder: contracts, releases bile
cards.section: Nerves and hormones run the line

cards.front: In healthy volunteers given CCK-8 at one dose, atropine cut the pancreatic trypsin response by 84%. At a higher, above-normal dose, atropine blocked less. What do these results suggest?
cards.back: At the first dose much of CCK's effect depended on acetylcholine, likely from nerves, not on CCK acting on the gland alone. At a higher dose atropine blocked less, so a smaller share depended on acetylcholine.
cards.why: Atropine blocks the acetylcholine receptors nerves use on many glands.
cards.quote: atropine, a drug that blocks the acetylcholine receptors nerves use on many glands, cut the pancreatic trypsin response by 84%.
cards.section: How much of CCK's effect needs nerves?

cards.front: An essential nutrient is one an animal must get from {{c1::food}} because its body cannot make it, or cannot make enough.
cards.quote: An essential nutrient is one an animal must get from food because its body cannot make it, or cannot make enough.
cards.section: Essential depends on who is eating

cards.front: Which two fatty acids are essential for humans?
cards.back: Linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid.
cards.quote: Two fatty acids are essential for humans, linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid.
cards.section: Essential depends on who is eating

cards.front: How many amino acids are essential for humans, and what are they?
cards.back: Nine: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine.
cards.quote: For humans, nine amino acids are essential: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine
cards.section: Essential depends on who is eating

cards.front: A rat and a guinea pig both eat a diet with no vitamin C for several weeks. Which one becomes deficient, and why?
cards.back: Only the guinea pig. Most mammals, rats included, make their own vitamin C; guinea pigs, like humans and some other primates, cannot.
cards.quote: Most mammals make their own vitamin C, but humans, some other primates and guinea pigs cannot and need it in the diet.
cards.section: Essential depends on who is eating

cards.front: Why must a domestic cat get taurine in its diet when an adult human does not?
cards.back: The cat, an obligate carnivore, needs taurine in its diet; adult humans and many other mammals make their own. Whether a nutrient is essential depends on the animal.
cards.quote: needs taurine, a small sulfur-containing compound related to amino acids, in its diet
cards.section: Essential depends on who is eating

cards.front: Does a cow need dietary vitamin B12 to the same degree as a human? Explain, and say what the cow still needs.
cards.back: No. Rumen microbes make B vitamins, including B12 when the diet contains cobalt. The needs do not vanish: the cow still needs cobalt.
cards.quote: Ruminant microbes make B vitamins, including B12 when the diet contains cobalt
cards.section: Essential depends on who is eating

cards.front: Microbial protein is made by microbes in a cow's rumen and in a horse's cecum and colon. Using the one-way rule, which animal is better placed to recover that protein, and why?
cards.back: Expected: the cow. Its microbes sit before the abomasum and small intestine, so their protein passes the main absorption site and is recovered as amino acids. A horse's microbes sit after it, so most of their protein is lost in its feces.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that a nutrient must be supplied before or within the stretch that can absorb it.
cards.quote: a nutrient must be supplied, by food or by microbes, before or within the stretch that can absorb it.
cards.section: Essential depends on who is eating

cards.front: Why does gut length track diet only loosely across mammals?
cards.back: Larger animals have longer intestines whatever they eat, and related species resemble each other through shared ancestry (phylogeny). With both accounted for, diet matters only loosely, and by region.
cards.quote: Larger animals have longer intestines whatever they eat, and related species resemble each other through shared ancestry, their phylogeny.
cards.section: Essential depends on who is eating

cards.front: Across mammal species, herbivores have longer large intestines than carnivores. Name four checks before concluding that eating plants lengthens the gut.
cards.back: 1) Scale by body mass. 2) Account for phylogeny: related species are not independent tests. 3) Test each gut region separately. 4) A cross-species correlation does not show cause; a feeding experiment within one species would test it.
cards.quote: fifty closely related herbivores are not fifty independent tests.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In many frogs, plant-eating tadpoles have a long coiled gut that shortens when the adult turns to eating animals. Why is this a poor test of whether diet changes gut length?
cards.back: Thyroid hormone drives the whole metamorphosis, so the diet change and the gut change are tangled; neither can be shown to cause the other.
cards.quote: thyroid hormone drives that whole transformation, so diet and gut change are tangled.
cards.section: Design problem
